title: The first three petitions (CCC 2803–2827)
hookLine: thy name, thy kingdom, thy will

cards: A wedding reception. The best man taps a glass, and for the whole first part of his speech he doesn't mention himself once. It's all about the couple: who they are, what they're building, what he hopes for them.
Only near the end does he get to himself, and even then it's mostly a thank-you. Nobody finds that strange. That's how speaking about someone you love tends to go.
The Catechism notices the Our Father is built the same way. Before a single request for ourselves, three lines in a row turn toward God. Today: the first three petitions.

teach.b: Listen to the little word that repeats, in the Douay-Rheims: "hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven." Thy, thy, thy.
The Catechism counts seven petitions, and says these first three draw us toward the Father's glory, for his own sake. It is the way of love, it says, to think first of the one we love. Thy name.
To hallow means to hold as holy. We don't make God holy by saying it; God's name already is. We ask that it be recognized as holy, and kept holy in us, in how we live.
Thy kingdom. Jesus began preaching with the kingdom at hand.

This petition looks first to the final coming of God's reign when Christ returns, and also to that kingdom growing now, quietly, wherever people live by the Spirit. Thy will. Here the prayer meets Gethsemane.

teach.h: THY WILL: NOT MINE, BUT THINE.
teach.b: On the night of his arrest Jesus prays, "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." He asks for what he wants. Then he hands it over.

And what is that will? The Catechism points to Paul: God "will have all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth." So the first half of the Our Father isn't small talk before the real requests.
In the Catholic reading, it reorders everything that comes after.

how: Catholics pray these three petitions every time they say the Our Father, at Mass, in the rosary and at home; some pause on 'thy will be done' when facing a hard decision.

games.q: what does “the first three petitions” mean?
o: three requests for our own daily needs
the Our Father's opening asks: thy name, kingdom, will
the three vows taken by monks, nuns and friars

games.q: thy, thy, thy — tap the pairs.
p: at Christ's return, and growing now
toward God, for his own sake

s: saying hallowed be thy name makes God holy
the Catechism says God's name already is holy; we ask that it be recognized and kept holy in us.
in Gethsemane Jesus asked for the chalice to pass before he handed it over
"Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done."
the Catechism says the kingdom petition is only about the far future
it looks first to Christ's return, and also to the kingdom growing now.

games.q: it's night in the garden. Jesus knows what's coming and doesn't want it. what does he pray?
o: only, take this away from me.
take it away, but not my will, thine.
games.why: he says honestly what he wants, then hands it over: "not my will, but thine be done." the third petition, prayed in the garden.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you want right now, honestly, the way Jesus did in the garden, and say it plainly inside.
If you pray, add his words, "not my will, but thine be done," and leave a long silence after them; if you don't, loosen your grip on it a little, the way you'd open a closed hand.

wordCard.voice: The first three petitions. In the Our Father: hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, thy will be done, the requests that turn toward God first, for his own sake.

orig.note: Greek: let it be hallowed, held holy — the first petition of the Our Father in Matthew 6:9.

carryVoice: Your line: thy, thy, thy. Love speaks of the one it loves first. See you tomorrow.
